title: Capstone Part 2: Deploy, Optimize, and Interview Prep
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Capstone Part 2: Deploy, Optimize, and Interview Prep

##### "Walk me through a system you've built"

A candidate in Bengaluru had genuinely strong work — an agentic RAG platform, deployed on Kubernetes, with evaluation gates in CI. In the interview he described it as: *"I built a RAG system using LangChain and vLLM with a reranker. It works well."*

The interviewer asked two follow-up questions and moved on.

A second candidate, weaker technically, described the same class of system: *"We had a 2-second TTFT budget and 8 QPS peak. I routed 70% of queries to a fast single-shot path and only escalated to the agent loop when document grading failed — that kept median latency at 1.8 seconds while handling multi-hop questions at 86% accuracy. The trade-off was p95 going to 8.4 seconds on the escalated 15%, which we accepted because those queries were previously unanswerable."*

She got the offer.

**The difference is not the system. It is the ability to state constraints, decisions, trade-offs, and measured outcomes.** That is also, not coincidentally, what distinguishes a production system from a working one.

Today ships the capstone and prepares you to talk about it.

##### Optimised serving

Part 1 built the core. Deployment starts with the optimisations from Days 31–34, applied in order of return.

```python
# Baseline first — you need the number to justify every change
BASELINE = {
    "config": "HF generate loop, fp16, no cache",
    "throughput_tok_s": 118,
    "ttft_p95_ms": 3_400,
    "cost_per_query_inr": 0.089,
    "gpu_count": 3,
}

OPTIMIZATION_LOG = [
    {"change": "vLLM with continuous batching + PagedAttention",
     "throughput_tok_s": 2_940, "ttft_p95_ms": 1_180,
     "cost_per_query_inr": 0.034, "gpu_count": 1,
     "note": "Day 31. Largest single win — 25x throughput."},

    {"change": "AWQ 4-bit quantization",
     "throughput_tok_s": 5_120, "ttft_p95_ms": 890,
     "cost_per_query_inr": 0.021, "gpu_count": 1,
     "note": "Day 33. Verified on golden set: 0.87 → 0.86 accuracy."},

    {"change": "Prefix caching on the 2.4k-token system prompt",
     "throughput_tok_s": 5_310, "ttft_p95_ms": 410,
     "cost_per_query_inr": 0.014, "gpu_count": 1,
     "note": "Day 32. One flag. Biggest TTFT improvement."},

    {"change": "Reduce top_k from 12 to 5",
     "throughput_tok_s": 6_890, "ttft_p95_ms": 340,
     "cost_per_query_inr": 0.009, "gpu_count": 1,
     "note": "Day 41. Accuracy IMPROVED 0.86 → 0.88 (less dilution)."},

    {"change": "Exact + semantic cache (0.97 threshold)",
     "throughput_tok_s": 6_890, "ttft_p95_ms": 340,
     "cost_per_query_inr": 0.006, "gpu_count": 1,
     "note": "Day 41. 31% hit rate on real traffic."},
]
```

**That table is your deliverable, not just your process.** It shows what each change bought, and the row where accuracy *improved* while cost fell is the one that demonstrates you measured rather than assumed.

**Verify quality after every optimisation.** Quantization and reduced context both change behaviour, and the regression gate from Day 36 is what tells you whether the change was free.

```python
def optimization_with_verification(name, apply_fn, eval_suite, gate,
                                   baseline_results):
    """Never ship a performance change without a quality check."""
    apply_fn()
    results = run_eval_suite(eval_suite)
    verdict = gate.check(results)

    return {
        "optimization": name,
        "quality_delta": round(results["overall_pass_rate"] -
                               baseline_results["overall_pass_rate"], 4),
        "blocked": verdict["blocked"],
        "regressions": verdict["regressions"],
        "ship": not verdict["blocked"],
    }
```

##### Production hardening

The checklist that turns a working deployment into one you can leave running.

```python
PRODUCTION_READINESS = {
    "reliability": [
        ("startupProbe with 15-min budget", "Day 43 — prevents restart loops"),
        ("maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1", "capacity never drops during rollout"),
        ("terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 180 + preStop", "drain in-flight streams"),
        ("Multi-zone, N+1 per zone", "survive a zonal GPU shortage"),
        ("Warm pool min_replicas: 2", "cold start is 7 min; cannot scale reactively"),
    ],
    "security": [
        ("Access control: pre-filter + post-verify", "Day 42 — enforced in code"),
        ("Capability restriction on untrusted content", "Day 37 — indirect injection"),
        ("Output sanitisation for markdown images", "the invisible exfil channel"),
        ("PII redaction before third-party calls", "reversible pseudonymisation"),
        ("Hash-chained audit log", "tamper-evident, PII-free"),
        ("Pinned model revisions, safetensors only", "supply chain"),
    ],
    "observability": [
        ("Tracing with SystemVersion fingerprint", "Day 35 — attributable changes"),
        ("Quality proxies: refusal rate, citations", "detects what latency cannot"),
        ("trace_id returned to callers", "makes complaints actionable"),
        ("Alerts with runbook links", "on-call should not improvise"),
        ("Daily drift check", "input distribution and retrieval scores"),
    ],
    "cost": [
        ("Budget cap enforced in code", "not just a dashboard alert"),
        ("Per-feature cost attribution", "Day 41 — cannot optimise unattributed spend"),
        ("Model cascade with verification", "80% of traffic on the cheap tier"),
        ("Batch API for nightly ingestion", "50% discount on non-urgent work"),
    ],
    "quality": [
        ("Blocking eval gate in CI", "Day 36 — zero tolerance on refusal cases"),
        ("Canary with quality-proxy analysis", "Day 43 — not just error rate"),
        ("Feedback → triage → eval set", "the loop that compounds"),
    ],
}
```

**The security section is where capstones most often fall short**, and it is what a senior reviewer checks first. A system with excellent retrieval and no tenant filter is not a production system.

##### The final evaluation report

Your practical task. This is the artefact that makes claims credible.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict
import json
import numpy as np


@dataclass
class EvaluationReport:
    system_fingerprint: str
    eval_date: str
    golden_set_size: int

    # Quality
    overall_pass_rate: float
    by_category: dict
    faithfulness: float
    context_recall: float
    hallucination_rate_unanswerable: float

    # Operational
    ttft_p50_ms: float
    ttft_p95_ms: float
    e2e_p95_s: float
    cost_per_query_inr: float
    cache_hit_rate: float

    # Security
    redteam_block_rate: float
    redteam_critical_failures: list
    access_control_violations: int
    false_positive_rate: float

    # Against requirements
    requirements_met: dict

    def summary_table(self) -> str:
        rows = [
            ("Answer accuracy", f"{self.overall_pass_rate:.1%}", "≥ 85%",
             self.overall_pass_rate >= 0.85),
            ("Hallucination (unanswerable)", f"{self.hallucination_rate_unanswerable:.1%}",
             "< 3%", self.hallucination_rate_unanswerable < 0.03),
            ("TTFT p95", f"{self.ttft_p95_ms:.0f}ms", "< 2000ms",
             self.ttft_p95_ms < 2000),
            ("E2E p95", f"{self.e2e_p95_s:.1f}s", "< 8s", self.e2e_p95_s < 8),
            ("Cost/query", f"₹{self.cost_per_query_inr:.4f}", "< ₹0.011",
             self.cost_per_query_inr < 0.011),
            ("Access violations", str(self.access_control_violations), "0",
             self.access_control_violations == 0),
            ("Red-team block rate", f"{self.redteam_block_rate:.1%}", "> 90%",
             self.redteam_block_rate > 0.90),
        ]
        lines = ["| Metric | Measured | Target | Met |", "|---|---|---|---|"]
        for name, measured, target, met in rows:
            lines.append(f"| {name} | {measured} | {target} | {'✅' if met else '❌'} |")
        return "\n".join(lines)
```

**Report against the requirements you set in Part 1.** A number without a target is trivia; a number next to the target you committed to is evidence.

**Include what you did not meet.** A report showing seven of eight targets met, with an honest explanation of the eighth, is far more credible than one claiming everything passed.

```python
LIMITATIONS = [
    {"limitation": "Multi-hop accuracy is 79%, below the 85% overall target",
     "cause": "Sequential retrieval on 3+ hop questions compounds errors",
     "mitigation": "Routed to human escalation when the agent loop exhausts "
                   "its iteration budget without confident grading",
     "next_step": "GraphRAG for the subset of queries that need traversal (Day 24)"},

    {"limitation": "Hindi query accuracy is 71% versus 88% English",
     "cause": "Embedding model is English-centric; corpus is 94% English",
     "mitigation": "Query translation to English before retrieval",
     "next_step": "Evaluate multilingual-e5 and IndicBERT for the retriever"},

    {"limitation": "p95 latency is 8.4s on the 15% of queries routed to the agent",
     "cause": "Iterative retrieval with grading, by design",
     "mitigation": "Streaming with progress indicators so the wait is visible",
     "next_step": "Parallel sub-query retrieval where dependencies allow"},
]
```

**A limitations section with causes, mitigations, and next steps** is the single strongest signal of engineering maturity in a portfolio project. It says you understand your own system.

##### The demo

```python
DEMO_STRUCTURE = {
    "0:00-0:30": {
        "content": "The problem, with a number",
        "script": "400 employees, 40,000 documents across three systems. "
                  "Finding a cross-functional answer took over 20 minutes.",
    },
    "0:30-1:30": {
        "content": "Live: a simple query and a hard one",
        "script": "Standard lookup with citations. Then a multi-hop comparison "
                  "that requires two documents — watch the trace show the "
                  "second retrieval.",
    },
    "1:30-2:00": {
        "content": "THE REFUSAL — show it saying 'I don't know'",
        "script": "Ask something the corpus does not cover. It refuses and "
                  "offers escalation rather than fabricating.",
    },
    "2:00-2:30": {
        "content": "Access control, demonstrated",
        "script": "Same query, two accounts in different departments. "
                  "Different results. Enforced in the retrieval filter, "
                  "not in the prompt.",
    },
    "2:30-3:30": {
        "content": "Architecture and one hard decision",
        "script": "The routing decision: 70% simple path at 1.8s, 15% agent "
                  "path at 8.4s p95. Why that trade-off was right.",
    },
    "3:30-4:30": {
        "content": "Results table and the optimisation log",
        "script": "Against the requirements set in the design doc. And the "
                  "row where reducing top_k improved accuracy AND cut cost.",
    },
    "4:30-5:00": {
        "content": "Limitations and what's next",
        "script": "Hindi accuracy gap, its cause, and the specific fix.",
    },
}
```

**Show the refusal.** It is more impressive than a correct answer because it demonstrates you thought about failure, and almost nobody demos it.

**Show the access control with two accounts.** It takes twenty seconds and it is the single clearest demonstration of production thinking.

##### System design interviews

The assignment. Two mock questions, and a structure that works.

**A structure for any GenAI system design question:**

```python
INTERVIEW_STRUCTURE = {
    "1_clarify": {
        "minutes": 5,
        "questions": [
            "What scale? Users, QPS, corpus size, growth rate?",
            "Latency budget — is this interactive or async?",
            "What accuracy is required, and what is the cost of being wrong?",
            "Multi-tenant? What are the access-control requirements?",
            "Data residency or compliance constraints?",
            "Build or buy — can we use hosted APIs, or must it be self-hosted?",
            "What does the team look like, and what is the timeline?",
        ],
        "why": "Never draw before you know the constraints. This alone "
               "separates senior from junior candidates.",
    },
    "2_requirements": {
        "minutes": 3,
        "output": "A quantified non-functional table — QPS, p95, cost, accuracy",
        "why": "Makes every later decision defensible against a number.",
    },
    "3_high_level": {
        "minutes": 10,
        "output": "Ingestion path, query path, observability, boundaries",
        "why": "Show the whole system before diving in.",
    },
    "4_deep_dive": {
        "minutes": 15,
        "follow_the_interviewer": True,
        "common_areas": ["chunking and retrieval", "access control",
                         "evaluation", "cost", "failure handling"],
    },
    "5_scale_and_cost": {
        "minutes": 8,
        "output": "Capacity arithmetic and a monthly cost estimate",
        "why": "Quantifying is what most candidates skip. Do the arithmetic aloud.",
    },
    "6_failure_modes": {
        "minutes": 5,
        "output": "What breaks, how you detect it, how you recover",
        "why": "Volunteer this before being asked.",
    },
}
```

**Mock question 1: "Design a RAG platform for a law firm with 2 million documents and 500 lawyers."**

Key things to surface:

```python
MOCK_1_KEY_POINTS = {
    "clarifying": [
        "Are documents client-confidential? → per-client access control is mandatory",
        "Is this used in billable work? → citations must be verifiable, "
        "hallucination is a professional liability",
        "Retention and privilege requirements?",
    ],
    "scale_arithmetic": (
        "2M documents × ~15 chunks = 30M chunks. Past pgvector's comfortable "
        "range — use a dedicated vector DB with HNSW, or IVF-PQ given the size "
        "(Day 23). 500 lawyers × 20 queries/day = 10k queries/day, ~2 QPS peak. "
        "Small QPS, large corpus — this is a retrieval-scale problem, not a "
        "serving-scale one."
    ),
    "critical_decisions": [
        "Per-client index namespaces, not metadata filters — privilege requires "
        "the strongest isolation available",
        "Hybrid search is mandatory: case citations, statute numbers, and "
        "clause references are lexical, not semantic",
        "Every claim must cite a document and paragraph; a refusal is always "
        "preferable to an unsupported answer",
        "Self-hosted or in-region: client confidentiality likely precludes "
        "third-party API processing",
    ],
    "failure_modes": [
        "Cross-client leakage → namespace isolation + post-verify + audit",
        "Hallucinated case citations → structured citation validation against "
        "the actual corpus, not just prompt instruction",
        "Stale documents after amendment → index versioning with recency filter",
    ],
}
```

**Mock question 2: "Design an agent that resolves customer support tickets autonomously."**

```python
MOCK_2_KEY_POINTS = {
    "clarifying": [
        "Autonomous meaning it takes actions, or drafts for human approval?",
        "What actions? Refunds and account changes are irreversible.",
        "What is the cost of a wrong action versus a missed resolution?",
        "Escalation path and volume?",
    ],
    "critical_decisions": [
        "Workflow with an agent escape hatch, not a pure agent (Day 30). "
        "Measure the deviation rate first — most tickets follow a fixed path.",
        "Human approval gate on every irreversible action (Day 37). "
        "Read-only tools by default; write tools require approval.",
        "Capability restriction: once the agent reads a customer-uploaded "
        "document, external-egress tools require approval regardless.",
        "Trajectory evaluation, not just outcome — an agent that resolves "
        "the ticket in 14 steps is a cost problem (Day 36).",
    ],
    "scale_and_cost": (
        "3,000 tickets/day. If 94% follow a standard path at ₹0.40 and 6% "
        "need the agent at ₹4.10, that is ₹1,866/day = ₹56k/month. A pure "
        "agent for all 3,000 would be ₹3.7 lakh/month."
    ),
    "failure_modes": [
        "Agent loops → iteration, token, and cost budgets, independently",
        "Prompt injection via ticket attachments → the defining risk; "
        "capability restriction is the defence, not detection",
        "Silent quality drift → refusal rate and thumbs-down monitoring",
    ],
}
```

**Do the arithmetic aloud.** "3,000 tickets at 94% cheap path" said out loud with numbers is what distinguishes a senior answer, and most candidates skip straight to boxes and arrows.

##### The conceptual questions

Twenty-five for the intermediate level. Write them out.

**Architecture and training**
1. Walk through a transformer's forward pass. Where do the parameters live?
2. Why did pre-norm replace post-norm?
3. Explain GQA. Compute the KV cache for a 7B model at 8k context, batch 32.
4. How does RoPE encode position, and why does naive extrapolation fail?
5. Explain MoE. Why does Mixtral hold 47B parameters but compute 13B?
6. Chinchilla versus Kaplan — what changed, and why do modern models train past compute-optimal?

**Adaptation**
7. When would you fine-tune rather than use RAG? Give a concrete example of each.
8. Explain LoRA. Why is B initialised to zeros, and how do you choose the rank?
9. What is catastrophic forgetting, and how do you detect it?
10. Explain DPO. Why did it largely replace PPO?
11. Walk through building an instruction dataset. What does LIMA suggest about size?

**RAG**
12. Your RAG system is at 71% accuracy. Walk me through diagnosing it.
13. Why hybrid search? Give a query where dense retrieval fails.
14. Explain parent-document retrieval and the problem it solves.
15. When does GraphRAG beat vector RAG? What does it cost?
16. Your context recall is 0.6 and faithfulness is 0.9. What do you fix?

**Production**
17. Explain PagedAttention and continuous batching.
18. Why is decode memory-bandwidth bound, and what follows from that?
19. How do you evaluate an LLM application? What is wrong with benchmark scores?
20. Explain indirect prompt injection and how you defend against it.
21. How would you cut an LLM feature's cost by 60%?
22. How do you implement multi-tenant access control in RAG?
23. What do you monitor, and what alerts would you set?
24. Walk through a canary deployment for a model update.
25. Tell me about a time your system gave a wrong answer. What did you do?

**Question 25 is the one that matters most.** Have a specific answer with the failure, how you detected it, the root cause, the fix, and how you verified it.

##### Portfolio presentation

```markdown
# Enterprise Knowledge Platform

**[Live demo](url)** · **[5-min video](url)** · **[Design doc](docs/design.md)** ·
**[Evaluation report](docs/evaluation.md)**

![architecture](docs/architecture.png)

## The problem
400 employees across 6 departments could not find answers spanning 40,000
documents in three systems. Cross-functional questions took 20+ minutes.

## Results against requirements

| Metric | Measured | Target | Met |
|---|---|---|---|
| Answer accuracy (120-case golden set) | 88.3% | ≥ 85% | ✅ |
| Hallucination rate (unanswerable) | 1.7% | < 3% | ✅ |
| TTFT p95 | 340ms | < 2000ms | ✅ |
| E2E p95 | 6.2s | < 8s | ✅ |
| Cost per query | ₹0.006 | < ₹0.011 | ✅ |
| Access control violations | 0 | 0 | ✅ |
| Red-team block rate | 94% | > 90% | ✅ |
| Multi-hop accuracy | 79% | ≥ 85% | ❌ (see limitations) |

## Optimisation log
[the table — showing top_k reduction improved accuracy AND cut cost]

## Key technical decisions
- **Query routing over pure agentic RAG** — 70% of queries take a 1.8s path;
  only 15% escalate. Pure agentic would have tripled median latency.
- **pgvector over a dedicated vector DB** — 180k chunks is well within range,
  and we already operate Postgres. Documented revisit trigger at 2M chunks.
- **Access control in the retrieval filter, with post-verification** — a prompt
  instruction is not a security boundary.

## Limitations
[the three, with cause / mitigation / next step]

## Run it
make setup && make ingest && make serve
```

**Lead with results against targets you committed to**, not with the tech stack. That table is what a hiring manager reads.

##### Career strategy

**Where intermediate GenAI roles concentrate in India:** Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, NCR, and Chennai, with a growing remote market. Product startups and AI-native companies weight portfolio heavily; larger enterprises and services companies still run DSA rounds alongside.

**What distinguishes an intermediate candidate from a beginner:**

| | Beginner signal | Intermediate signal |
|---|---|---|
| RAG | "I built a RAG system" | "Context recall was the bottleneck at 0.62; hybrid search took it to 0.84" |
| Cost | Not mentioned | "₹0.006 per query, down from ₹0.089, with the optimisation log" |
| Failure | "It works well" | "Here is where it fails, why, and what I would fix" |
| Evaluation | "I tested it" | "120-case golden set with 20% unanswerable, blocking gate in CI" |
| Security | Not mentioned | "Access control in the retrieval filter, with post-verification and a test" |

**Staying current — three hours a week:**

- One paper skimmed properly: abstract, figures, conclusion, then decide.
- One thing built. Reading about a technique is not knowing it.
- Follow a few practitioners rather than the timeline. Simon Willison, Sebastian Raschka, Lilian Weng, the Hugging Face daily papers.

**Ignore:** most Twitter and LinkedIn hype, and anything claiming last month's technique is obsolete. The fundamentals from Days 1–6 have been stable since 2017.

**Visibility compounds.** A blog post explaining one hard decision from your capstone is a portfolio piece, an interview rehearsal, and a networking artefact simultaneously. Two or three good posts beat twenty shallow ones, and referrals convert several times better than cold applications.

##### The completion checklist

- [ ] Deployed with optimised serving (vLLM, quantization, caching)
- [ ] Optimisation log showing what each change bought
- [ ] Guardrails: input, output, capability restriction, access control
- [ ] Red-team report with block rate and false-positive rate
- [ ] Evaluation report against the Part 1 requirements
- [ ] Limitations section with cause, mitigation, and next step
- [ ] Tracing live, with `trace_id` returned and a metrics dashboard
- [ ] Blocking eval gate in CI
- [ ] Canary deployment configured with quality-proxy analysis
- [ ] Runbooks for the three most likely incidents
- [ ] Public URL that works right now
- [ ] 5-minute demo video, rehearsed
- [ ] README leading with results against targets
- [ ] 25 interview questions answered in writing
- [ ] Two system design mocks completed and written up
- [ ] Someone outside your team has used it successfully

##### Common mistakes

- **Describing systems without constraints, decisions, or numbers** — the interview that ended in two questions.
- **Optimising without verifying quality** after each change.
- **No limitations section**, which reads as inexperience.
- **Demoing only the happy path.**
- **Skipping the clarifying questions** in system design and drawing immediately.
- **No cost arithmetic** in a design interview.
- **Claiming your system never failed.** Nobody believes it.
- **A README leading with the tech stack** instead of results.
- **No live URL**, so nobody sees it working.
- **Security omitted from the capstone** — the first thing a senior reviewer checks.
- **Rehearsing the demo once.** Record it three times minimum.

##### Hands-on: ship it and rehearse

Your practical task deploys with optimised serving, guardrails, and monitoring, then produces the evaluation report. Run the full evaluation twice — before and after your optimisation pass — so the report shows both the final numbers and what the optimisations cost or gained in quality. The row where a cost reduction improved accuracy is the one worth highlighting.

The mini project ships the complete system with a live demo, architecture docs, and a metrics dashboard. Send the URL to someone who has never seen it and watch them use it for five minutes without helping. You will find three problems, and fixing them is worth more than another optimisation.

The assignment completes two system design mocks and writes up your solutions. Do them **out loud with a timer**, ideally with someone playing interviewer. Then write up each with the clarifying questions you asked, the requirements you derived, the architecture, the capacity arithmetic, and the failure modes. That written record is both interview preparation and a portfolio artefact.

##### Key takeaways

- **State constraints, decisions, trade-offs, and measured outcomes.** That is what separates a strong interview answer from a weak one describing the same system.
- **Verify quality after every performance optimisation** — and report the change where reducing cost also improved accuracy, because it proves you measured.
- **Report against the targets you committed to in Part 1**, including the ones you missed, with cause and next step.
- **Demo the refusal and the access control.** Twenty seconds each, and together they demonstrate more production thinking than any feature.
- **In system design, clarify before you draw and do the arithmetic aloud** — quantifying scale and cost is the step most candidates skip and the one interviewers remember.
